For a star with twenty times the mass of our sun, death is more dramatic. The core of such a
star collapses inward. Temperatures reach 100 billion degrees. The crushing force of gravity
is unstoppable. Massive hunks of iron are compacted instantly into grains of sand. Atoms are
shattered into electrons, protons and neutrons, and those particles are shattered into even
tinier bits, quarks and leptons. Eventually, the star transforms into a black hole.
A black hole, however, is anything but empty space. It is a great amount of matter packed
into a very small area — think of a star ten times more massive than the Sun squeezed into a
sphere the diameter of New York City. What makes a black hole so incredible is the speed
needed to escape its gravitational pull. To overcome Earth's gravity, you must accelerate to
about seven miles a second. That's very fast, but human-built rockets have been escaping
Earth’s gravitational pull and heading into space since 1959. Now consider light — the fastest
thing in the universe — which travels at an incredible 186,282 miles a second. Even so, it
can't defeat the gravitational pull of a black hole. A black hole is also a place separated from
the rest of the universe. The dividing line between the inside and outside of a black hole is
called the event horizon. Anything crossing the horizon — a Star, a planet —is making a one-
way trip.
In the early twentieth century, Albert Einstein considered the Possibility of black holes. His
formulas allowed for their existence, but the idea that gravity could overwhelm all cian

It was during the 1960s that scientific investigation really progressed as scientists began
inventing new ways of looking into space. Using existing X-ray and radio-wave technology,
they were able to develop telescopes that were far more powerful than ever before, and
which allowed astronomers to see more accurately the workings of galaxies”. They found
that at the centre of billions of galaxies in the universe is a crowded lump of stars, and a
mixture of different gases. They also realised that it was dust, essential along with gas for
creating stars, that makes it impossible to observe the centre of a galaxy with the naked eye.
At the very centre of virtually every galaxy looked at is an object so heavy and so compact,
with such strong gravitational pull, that there is only one possible explanation: it is a black
hole.
These black holes are huge. The one at the centre of our own galaxy, the Milky Way, is
4.3 million times as heavy as the Sun. The mass of the black hole in the galaxy Andromeda
is equal to 100 million suns. Black hole experts believe that small holes are located
throughout the universe. Indeed, the current thinking is that they may well number in the
trillions, although this is yet to be proved.
Most experts agree that black holes are real. They also acknowledge that they do more than
merely exist; black holes help create the fabric of the universe. Objects heading in the
direction of a black hole produce friction in huge quantities. Black holes revolve, and
because of this spin a significant amount of the matter falling toward a black hole, sometimes
more than 90 percent of it, does not pass through the event horizon, but rather is flung off in
another direction. From here it has the potential to become new stars.
It is important to note that a black hole has no more vacuuming power than a regular star.
Imagine if our sun were to become a black hole; it would keep the same mass yet its
diameter would shrink from 865,000 miles to less than four miles. Earth would be dark and
cold, but our orbit around the sun wouldn't change. Also, we already know from physicists
that time is ‘relative’ - meaning it doesn’t move at the same speed for everybody. So if
anyone could spend a minute close by the event horizon of a black hole and were able to
suddenly return to Earth, they would discover that a thousand years had passed. And what
would happen if you were pulled inside? Scientists can only speculate.
